effort.activeTime: ~15-30 minutes to register; a few hours to implement and test the flow
effort.waitTime: none for the OAuth app itself (optional Marketplace publisher verification has an unstated review time)

steps.title: Choose OAuth App vs GitHub App
steps.detail: GitHub generally recommends GitHub Apps over OAuth apps: GitHub Apps use fine-grained permissions, while OAuth apps use coarse scopes (e.g. issue or pull request access needs the broad 'repo' scope). The main exception is when you need enterprise-level resources, which GitHub Apps can't yet get. This guide covers the OAuth app path.

steps.title: Decide the owning account
steps.detail: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps. Register under an organization if you may later sell paid plans on GitHub Marketplace; only org-owned apps can be verified publishers, and personal-owned apps must be transferred first.

steps.title: Register the OAuth app
steps.detail: Profile picture > Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps > New OAuth App ('Register a new application' if it's your first). For an org: the organization's Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps. Fill in Application name, Homepage URL, optional description, and Authorization callback URL (use 'Add callback URL' for more, up to 10). Leave 'Expire user access tokens' enabled (default) if your app can handle refresh tokens; tick 'Enable Device Flow' only if needed. Click Register application.

steps.title: Copy the Client ID and generate a client secret
steps.detail: After creation, copy the Client ID and generate a client secret. Store the secret securely; it is required in the token exchange.

steps.title: Choose minimal scopes
steps.detail: Pick the narrowest scopes from 'Scopes for OAuth apps' (e.g. no scope for public info, public_repo instead of repo, user:email for private emails). Requested scopes are shown on the authorization form. Source code access cannot be scoped to read-only.

steps.title: Implement the web application flow with PKCE
steps.detail: Redirect users to https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize with client_id (required), and the strongly recommended redirect_uri, state, code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256 (plain is not accepted), plus scope. Exchange the code at POST https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token with client_id, client_secret, code, the same redirect_uri, and code_verifier (required if a code_challenge was sent).

steps.title: Handle token expiry and refresh
steps.detail: With expiring tokens, access tokens last 8 hours (expires_in=28800) and refresh tokens expire after 6 months of non-use. Refresh with grant_type=refresh_token; each refresh returns a new pair and invalidates the old one, and cannot change scopes. Requesting the offline_access scope yields expiring tokens plus a refresh token even if the app isn't configured for them.

steps.title: Verify granted scopes
steps.detail: Check the X-OAuth-Scopes response header for the scopes the token actually has, and X-Accepted-OAuth-Scopes for what an endpoint requires. Users may grant fewer scopes than requested.

steps.title: Test with an external account, including an org member
steps.detail: Authorize with a second GitHub account outside your org and confirm access to its org-owned resources. OAuth app access restrictions are on by default for new organizations, so an org owner must approve your app before it can reach private org resources.

steps.title: (Optional) Publisher verification and Marketplace listing
steps.detail: Only needed to offer paid plans or show a Marketplace badge: organization Settings > Developer settings > Publisher Verification, complete the checklist (accurate profile and support email, org 2FA, verified domain), then click Request Verification. Not required for users to authorize your app.

gotchas: OAuth scopes are coarse: 'repo' grants full read/write to all public and private repos plus some org resources.
Source code access cannot be scoped to read-only with OAuth app scopes.

Redirect URL matching: with wildcard matching disabled the redirect_uri must exactly match a registered callback URL; with it enabled, host (ignoring subdomains) and port must match and the path must be a subdirectory. Apps with a single callback URL created before August 3, 2026 have wildcard matching on by default; GitHub recommends disabling it if not needed. Loopback redirect URLs may use a different port.
If redirect_uri is omitted, GitHub sends users to the first configured callback URL.
Users can grant fewer scopes than requested; check X-OAuth-Scopes rather than assuming.
OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default for new organizations: unapproved apps see only public org resources until an owner approves.
Orgs using SAML SSO require the user to have an active SAML session when authorizing.
Users must have a verified email address before authorizing an OAuth app.

GitHub issues at most 10 tokens per user/application/scope combination and allows 10 token creations per hour; exceeding the 10-token cap silently revokes an older token, so don't re-run the flow per session.

REST API rate limit for OAuth user tokens is 5,000 requests/hour per user, shared with that user's other apps and PATs (15,000/hour when the app is owned or approved by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud org the user belongs to).
Implicit grant and CORS preflight requests are not supported, so the token exchange must happen server-side.

approval.process: No GitHub review is needed for external users to authorize an OAuth app. Per-organization owner approval may be needed for access to private org resources (restrictions are on by default for new orgs). Optional publisher verification (org profile/support email, org 2FA, verified domain, then 'Request Verification') is only required to offer paid Marketplace plans or display a Marketplace badge.
rejectionRisks: For publisher verification: missing or inaccurate org profile/support email
For publisher verification: org 2FA not enabled
For publisher verification: no verified domain badge on the org profile
App owned by a personal account when trying to become a verified publisher

blockers.issue: End users' organizations block your app via OAuth app access restrictions (default for new orgs), so private org repos are invisible to the agent.
blockers.whatToDo: Tell users to request org owner approval during authorization, or switch to a GitHub App that orgs install explicitly.

blockers.issue: redirect_uri mismatch errors during authorization or token exchange.
blockers.whatToDo: Register every exact callback URL (up to 10), send the same redirect_uri in the token request, and don't rely on wildcard subdirectory matching unless it's enabled for the app.
Store and use the refresh token (valid 6 months of non-use), or clear 'Expire user access tokens' if your app can't yet handle refresh.
Reuse stored tokens instead of re-authorizing; GitHub keeps at most 10 tokens per user/app/scope and revokes extras.

blockers.issue: Scopes too broad (e.g. repo) deter users or security reviewers.
blockers.whatToDo: Request minimal scopes or move to a GitHub App with fine-grained permissions.

blockers.issue: Wanting to sell on Marketplace but the app is owned by a personal account.
blockers.whatToDo: Transfer app ownership to an organization where you are an owner, then complete publisher verification.
